quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The feedback from my colleagues ___ I received after the presentation was surprisingly positive.
quests.completedSentence: The feedback from my colleagues (no word needed) I received after the presentation was surprisingly positive.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I received' the feedback, not the colleagues themselves - this is an object relative clause modifying 'the feedback,' so the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'From my colleagues' just tells you the source - check what 'I' actually received.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: The offer from the other company ___ ultimately convinced her to switch jobs.
quests.completedSentence: The offer from the other company which ultimately convinced her to switch jobs.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The offer' - not 'the company' - is what convinced her, so this is a subject relative clause; the pronoun cannot be dropped, and 'which' is correct since an offer is a thing.
quests.nativeTip: 'From the other company' just tells you the source - check what actually did the convincing.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The concerns ___ residents raised at the town hall meeting went unresolved for months.
quests.completedSentence: The concerns (no word needed) residents raised at the town hall meeting went unresolved for months.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Residents' is the subject of 'raised,' so 'the concerns' is the object being raised; since concerns are things, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'Residents' already has a job in this clause - 'raised.' What does that leave for the concerns, and does the pronoun even need to stay?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The professor who wrote the textbook we used all semester later won a national teaching award. What does the omitted clause 'we used all semester' describe?
quests.completedSentence: The professor who wrote the textbook we used all semester later won a national teaching award. What does the omitted clause 'we used all semester' describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'We used' the textbook, not the professor or the award, so 'the textbook' is the antecedent of this omitted object relative clause.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward - what did 'we' actually use all semester?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: The engineer ___ designed the bridge we cross every day used to work for the city.
quests.completedSentence: The engineer who designed the bridge we cross every day used to work for the city.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Designed' has no other subject, so 'the engineer' must supply it - the pronoun cannot be dropped here, and 'who' is correct since the engineer is a person.
quests.nativeTip: Check the first gap: does 'designed' already have a subject elsewhere in the sentence?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which of the sentences shown is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: The teacher who assigned the essay we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet.
quests.completedSentence: Which of the sentences shown is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who assigned the essay' correctly keeps 'who' since it's a subject relative clause about a person; 'we submitted yesterday' correctly drops its pronoun since it's an object relative clause about a thing.
quests.nativeTip: Check both clauses separately: one needs its pronoun to stay, and the other has correctly dropped it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The teacher who assigned the essay we submitted yesterday hasn't graded it yet."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: No Relative Clause Needed (Hypercorrection)
quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: I bought a new phone yesterday.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a simple sentence with no relative clause at all - there's no second noun being described by a clause, so no relative pronoun belongs here. Inserting 'that,' 'which,' or 'who' breaks the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Not every sentence needs a relative pronoun - check whether this sentence is even describing one noun with extra information about it.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "I bought a new phone yesterday."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: No Relative Clause Needed (Hypercorrection)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly completes this idea, if any relative pronoun is even needed: 'She adopted a rescue dog last spring'?
quests.targetClause: She adopted a rescue dog last spring.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly completes this idea, if any relative pronoun is even needed: 'She adopted a rescue dog last spring'?
quests.ruleExplanation: This sentence simply states what she did - there's no additional noun being described by a clause, so no relative pronoun is needed anywhere in the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Ask yourself: is there a second noun anywhere in this sentence that needs its own describing clause?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "She adopted a rescue dog last spring."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly completes this idea: 'She adopted a rescue dog. The dog had been abandoned twice before.'?
quests.targetClause: She adopted a rescue dog that had been abandoned twice before.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly completes this idea: 'She adopted a rescue dog. The dog had been abandoned twice before.'?
quests.ruleExplanation: Unlike the previous example, this sentence needs a relative clause to add the fact that the dog had been abandoned; since 'had been abandoned' has no other subject, the pronoun 'that' must stay.
quests.nativeTip: This time, there genuinely IS a second idea describing the dog - check where the connecting word belongs and whether it can be dropped.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "She adopted a rescue dog that had been abandoned twice before."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: No Relative Clause Needed (Hypercorrection)
quests.questionSentence: Which one of these sentences is correctly written?
quests.targetClause: The team finished the project ahead of schedule.
quests.completedSentence: Which one of these sentences is correctly written?
quests.ruleExplanation: This is a complete, simple sentence describing what the team did - there's no relative clause needed here at all.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether this sentence has a second noun anywhere that needs extra description via a clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The team finished the project ahead of schedule."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: No Relative Clause Needed (Hypercorrection)
quests.questionSentence: Which version here is grammatically correct?
quests.targetClause: The results of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting.
quests.completedSentence: Which version here is grammatically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The results of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting' is already a complete, correct sentence; inserting 'that' or 'which' either creates a sentence fragment or unnecessarily complicates a sentence that needs no relative clause.
quests.nativeTip: This is a simple statement about what the results did - check whether any noun here truly needs an extra describing clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The results of the survey surprised everyone at the meeting."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The results of the survey ___ our team conducted last quarter surprised everyone at the meeting.
quests.completedSentence: The results of the survey (no word needed) our team conducted last quarter surprised everyone at the meeting.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Our team' is the subject of 'conducted,' so 'the results' is the object being conducted upon; since results are things, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely: 'the results our team conducted.'
quests.nativeTip: 'Our team' already has a job in this clause - 'conducted.' What does that leave for the results, and does the pronoun even need to stay?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which version fits a formal business report?
quests.targetClause: The vendor that we selected offers better pricing.
quests.completedSentence: Which version fits a formal business report?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That we selected' is the fully written, formal version appropriate for a business report; the pronoun is retained rather than dropped.
quests.nativeTip: Formal reports generally spell out every grammatical element rather than relying on casual shortcuts.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The vendor that we selected offers better pricing."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which version would you most likely text a friend?
quests.targetClause: The apartment we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!
quests.completedSentence: Which version would you most likely text a friend?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The apartment we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!' is the shortest, most natural phrasing for a casual text, dropping the object relative pronoun entirely.
quests.nativeTip: Texts tend to be short and casual - which option drops the unnecessary connecting word?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The apartment we toured yesterday had amazing natural light!"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Whether you're texting a friend or writing a formal report, which version of this sentence is always correct?
quests.targetClause: The vendor that offers better pricing raised concerns among the team.
quests.completedSentence: Whether you're texting a friend or writing a formal report, which version of this sentence is always correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'the vendor' is the subject of 'offers' (no other candidate exists), the relative pronoun must stay in every register - casual or formal. 'That' correctly introduces this subject relative clause.
quests.nativeTip: Unlike object relative clauses, this type of clause never allows the pronoun to be dropped - not even informally.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The vendor that offers better pricing raised concerns among the team."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains an error?
quests.targetClause: The car needs repairs is parked outside.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains an error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Needs repairs' has no other subject - 'the car' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped there.
quests.nativeTip: Look for a clause that needs its own subject but doesn't have one supplied anywhere.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The car needs repairs is parked outside."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: No Relative Clause Needed (Hypercorrection)
quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences has an error?
quests.targetClause: I called that the mechanic yesterday.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences has an error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I called that the mechanic yesterday' incorrectly inserts 'that' into what should be a simple sentence - there's no relative clause here at all, so 'that' doesn't belong.
quests.nativeTip: Look for a sentence where a connecting word has been added even though there's no second noun being described by a clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "I called that the mechanic yesterday."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence below contains a mistake?
quests.targetClause: The package arrived yesterday was damaged.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence below contains a mistake?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Arrived yesterday' has no subject of its own - 'the package' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped; it should read 'The package that arrived yesterday was damaged.'
quests.nativeTip: Three of these are correct - either they have no relative clause at all, or they correctly keep or drop the pronoun based on its role. Only one breaks the rule.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The package arrived yesterday was damaged."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The diagnosis the specialist ultimately confirmed matched her initial symptoms perfectly. What is the antecedent of the omitted clause 'the specialist ultimately confirmed'?
quests.completedSentence: The diagnosis the specialist ultimately confirmed matched her initial symptoms perfectly. What is the antecedent of the omitted clause 'the specialist ultimately confirmed'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The specialist confirmed' the diagnosis, so 'the diagnosis' is the antecedent of this omitted object relative clause.
quests.nativeTip: Work backward - what did the specialist actually confirm?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: The witness statement ___ contradicted the officer's report troubled the jury.
quests.completedSentence: The witness statement which contradicted the officer's report troubled the jury.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Contradicted' has no other subject - 'the witness statement' must supply it, so the pronoun cannot be dropped; since a statement is a thing, 'which' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'contradicted' already has a subject elsewhere - if not, this pronoun must stay.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The contract clause ___ our attorneys spent weeks negotiating finally satisfied both parties.
quests.completedSentence: The contract clause (no word needed) our attorneys spent weeks negotiating finally satisfied both parties.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Our attorneys' is the subject of 'spent... negotiating,' so 'the contract clause' is the object being negotiated; since a clause is a thing, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'Our attorneys' already has a job in this clause - 'spent weeks negotiating.' What does that leave for the clause itself, and does the pronoun need to stay?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The testimony of the witness the defense team thoroughly cross-examined ultimately swayed the verdict. What is the true antecedent of the omitted clause 'the defense team thoroughly cross-examined'?
quests.completedSentence: The testimony of the witness the defense team thoroughly cross-examined ultimately swayed the verdict. What is the true antecedent of the omitted clause 'the defense team thoroughly cross-examined'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The defense team cross-examined' the witness - a person - not the testimony directly, so 'the witness' is the true antecedent of this omitted object relative clause, despite 'testimony' appearing first in the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what the defense team actually cross-examined - was it the testimony itself, or the person who gave it?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The recommendation from the panel of experts ___ the board is expected to approve next week has sparked internal debate.
quests.completedSentence: The recommendation from the panel of experts (no word needed) the board is expected to approve next week has sparked internal debate.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The board' is the subject of 'is expected to approve,' so 'the recommendation' is the object; since a recommendation is a thing, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'Of experts' just tells you whose panel it is - and 'the board' already has a job in this clause. What does that leave for the recommendation, and does the pronoun need to stay?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The findings of the investigation ___ ultimately confirmed every allegation.
quests.completedSentence: The findings of the investigation which ultimately confirmed every allegation.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The findings' - not 'the investigation' - is what confirmed every allegation, so this is a subject relative clause; the pronoun cannot be dropped, and 'which' is correct since findings are things.
quests.nativeTip: 'Of the investigation' just tells you which findings - check what actually did the confirming.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Clause with who
quests.questionSentence: The negotiator ___ handled the merger talks earned a substantial bonus.
quests.completedSentence: The negotiator who handled the merger talks earned a substantial bonus.
quests.ruleExplanation: Nothing else performs 'handled,' so 'the negotiator' must be its subject - 'who' is correct.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether 'handled' already has a subject elsewhere in the sentence.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Omission of Object Relative Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: The merger ___ the negotiator handled for months finally closed.
quests.completedSentence: The merger (no word needed) the negotiator handled for months finally closed.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The negotiator' is the subject of 'handled,' so 'the merger' is the object; since a merger is a thing, none of the personal pronouns fit, and the pronoun can be dropped entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'The negotiator' already has a job in this clause - 'handled.' What does that leave for the merger, and does the pronoun need to stay?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: The negotiator ___ reputation was built on tough deals rarely lost a client.
quests.completedSentence: The negotiator whose reputation was built on tough deals rarely lost a client.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whose' is correct because the reputation belongs to the negotiator; this shows possession, not an action performed directly.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what belongs to the negotiator, rather than what the negotiator is doing to someone else.

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The summary of the findings the lead researcher personally verified appeared in the final report. What is the true antecedent of the omitted clause 'the lead researcher personally verified'?
quests.completedSentence: The summary of the findings the lead researcher personally verified appeared in the final report. What is the true antecedent of the omitted clause 'the lead researcher personally verified'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The lead researcher verified' the findings, not the summary directly, so 'the findings' is the true antecedent of this omitted object relative clause.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what the lead researcher actually verified - the summary itself, or the underlying findings it's based on?

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which one of these sentences has a grammatical mistake?
quests.targetClause: The senator sponsored the bill received national attention.
quests.completedSentence: Which one of these sentences has a grammatical mistake?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Sponsored the bill' has no other subject - 'the senator' must supply it, so the relative pronoun cannot be dropped; it should read 'The senator who sponsored the bill received national attention.'
quests.nativeTip: Three of these sentences are correct for different reasons - either no clause is needed, or the pronoun's presence or absence correctly matches its role. Only one breaks the rule.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The senator sponsored the bill received national attention."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.grammarRule: Subject Relative Pronoun Cannot Be Omitted
quests.questionSentence: Which version of this sentence would be a grammatical error no matter the register - formal or casual?
quests.targetClause: The policy sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families.
quests.completedSentence: Which version of this sentence would be a grammatical error no matter the register - formal or casual?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The policy sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families' incorrectly drops the subject relative pronoun - since 'the policy' is the subject of 'sparked' and there's no other candidate, this pronoun can never be dropped, in any register.
quests.nativeTip: Unlike object relative clauses, one type of relative clause always needs its pronoun, no matter how casual the setting.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The policy sparked nationwide debate affected millions of families."
